turns.doctor_question: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?
turns.patient_response: Hi, doctor. Well, what brings me in is that I just keep planning my days around not having to drive over high bridges. I'll take these long detours just to avoid them. And if I absolutely can't get around it and have to cross one, I just white-knuckle it the whole way across. It's just getting to be a bit much to deal with.

symptom_reasoning.S064: The patient describes taking long detours to avoid driving over high bridges and 'white-knuckling' it when forced to cross, confirming active avoidance and enduring the phobic situation with intense distress.

turns.doctor_question: When you think about crossing a high bridge, what specifically frightens you the most — is it the height itself, or is it something else like being trapped or losing control of the car?
turns.patient_response: Well, I guess it's not really about being trapped. I mean, I know those big bridges over the bay are built fine, and folks drive over them every single day without a problem. But when I get near one, my mind just... it acts like the car could go right over the side. That's what really gets to me.

symptom_reasoning.S062: The patient describes marked, irrational fear about driving over high bridges, recognizing that the bridges are safe yet experiencing persistent fear of driving over the edge.

turns.doctor_question: Besides high bridges, are there other situations involving heights that make you anxious — like being on a tall building, a balcony, or even just looking out a window from a high floor?
turns.patient_response: No, not really. I mean, I can go up to a high floor in a building or look out a window just fine. Balconies don't bother me either. It's... it's really just the driving over those high bridges that gets to me. That's the only time I feel that way.

turns.doctor_question: If someone else were driving and you were a passenger crossing a high bridge, would you feel the same anxiety, or is it specifically about you being behind the wheel?
turns.patient_response: You know, I'm not really sure. I haven't been a passenger over one of those bridges in... well, I can't even remember how long. I usually do the driving. So, I don't really know if it would be any different if someone else was behind the wheel.

turns.doctor_question: I know you haven't been a passenger over a high bridge in a long time, but let me ask — if you were to sit in the passenger seat while someone else drove over one of those high bridges, do you think you'd feel that same fear about the car going over the side, or do you think it would be less anxiety since you're not the one driving?
turns.patient_response: I guess... I really just don't know. Like I said, it's been so long since I've been in that situation. I'd like to think it would be better if I wasn't the one steering, but honestly, I can't say for sure how I'd react. I just try to avoid the whole thing altogether.

symptom_reasoning.S064: The patient reports actively avoiding high bridges entirely ('I just try to avoid the whole thing altogether').

turns.doctor_question: Let me ask it a different way — if you were a passenger and someone else was driving, and the car started to approach a high bridge, do you think you'd still feel that fear about the car going over the side, or would that fear pretty much go away?
turns.patient_response: I honestly just don't know. I mean... I really can't say if the fear would go away or not. I haven't done it, so I can't tell you how I'd feel. I just don't know.

turns.doctor_question: When you're driving on a regular road at ground level, even if that road is long or somewhat dangerous in other ways, do you feel that same kind of anxiety about the car going over the side?
turns.patient_response: No, not at all. If I'm just driving on a regular road, even if it's a long trip or there's a lot of traffic, I'm completely fine. I don't worry about going off the side or anything like that. It's really just those high bridges that get to me. Regular roads don't bother me a bit.

turns.doctor_question: Let me try to make this more concrete. Imagine you're sitting in the passenger seat, completely relaxed, and your spouse or a trusted friend is driving smoothly over a high bridge. In that scenario, as you're looking out at the height and the water below, do you think that fear about the car going over the side would still come up for you?
turns.patient_response: Even picturing it like that... I still can't give you a straight yes or no. I mean, it sounds nice to think I'd be relaxed if my wife was driving, but the truth is, I haven't put myself in that spot for years. I might tense up and still panic about us going over the edge, or I might be okay. I just don't have a way to know without actually getting in the passenger seat and doing it.

turns.doctor_question: I understand you haven't been a passenger in years, but let me ask you this directly: When you imagine yourself as a passenger with your wife driving smoothly and safely over a high bridge, and you're just sitting there looking at the view — do you think your body would still have that physical panic reaction, or do you think you'd stay calm?
turns.patient_response: I... I really just don't know how else to say it, Doc. I honestly can't tell you. I mean, maybe my body would still react and I'd get that panic, or maybe I'd be fine because I'm not the one steering. But since I haven't actually done it in so long, I just can't give you a straight answer on what would happen. I really don't know.

turns.doctor_question: If you were a passenger in your wife's car crossing a high bridge, would you experience anxiety about the car going over the side?
turns.patient_response: Look, Doc, I feel like we're going in circles a bit here. Like I just said, I really don't know. I haven't been a passenger on a bridge in years, so I can't tell you if I'd still have that fear about going over the edge or not. I'd just be making it up if I gave you a yes or no answer.

turns.doctor_question: Let me ask you this differently — when you think about being a passenger, does the idea of being in a car you're not controlling make you feel less anxious about going over a bridge, or does the height of the bridge itself seem just as scary regardless of who's driving?
turns.patient_response: Honestly, I'm just not sure. I mean, not being the one steering... maybe that would take some of the pressure off. But then again, a bridge is a bridge, and the drop is still right there. I really haven't noticed if one thought is scarier than the other. I just know I avoid the whole situation entirely, so I can't really say which part of it would be worse if I was sitting in the passenger seat.

symptom_reasoning.S064: The patient explicitly confirms active phobic avoidance by stating that they avoid the whole situation (bridges) entirely.
